item.title: Restricted triangular ice beyond the solvable manifolds: chiral ice and the critical region of dominant chiral vertices
item.description: arXiv:2611.03760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study two restrictions of Baxter's symmetric twenty-vertex model on the triangular lattice, in which the three classes of vertices allowed by the ice rule carry the weights $a$, $b$ and $c$: chiral ice, in which only the twelve chiral vertices are allowed, and the model that excludes only the two alternating vertices. We show that neither model belongs to any of the known exactly solvable families of the twenty-vertex model, and we characterise chiral ice as the ice model in which every vertex has exactly one through line, a property that imposes a parity constraint along every closed lattice line. We compute the residual entropies of both models with transfer matrices on cylinders of up to twelve vertices in circumference, extrapolated with the finite-size correction predicted by conformal invariance, which we adapt to the triangular geometry and verify at two exactly solved points. The number of upward arrows crossing the cylinder is conserved, and the cost of changing it shows that both models are critical, with the long-distance behaviour of a free massless field. Chiral ice is the extreme point of a region of the phase diagram in which ordering had been suggested; along two paths through that region we find the same critical behaviour at every point, with no feature at the proposed boundary of the region. Along Baxter's exactly solved curve we obtain the corresponding exponents in closed form.
item.dc:creator: Josep Batle

item.title: The Inverse Mean First-Passage Time Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.03831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the mean first-passage time $\tau(x)$ for an overdamped particle in a one-dimensional potential landscape, and address the problem inverse to the textbook one: Given $\tau(x)$ as a function of starting distance, we look for a potential that realizes it. We derive the conditions on $\tau(x)$ under which such a potential exists. We show that while the power-law dependences $\tau(x)\sim x^\alpha$ with $\alpha \leq 2$ may be realized by monotonic potentials, any realizable $\tau(x)$ with superquadratic growth requires potential wells arbitrarily far from the target; $\alpha = 2$ separates sliding from trapping-dominated motion regimes.
item.dc:creator: Tommer D. Keidar, Shlomi Reuveni, Igor M. Sokolov

item.title: Lattice spin systems coupled to a compact U(1) gauge field with negative gauge coupling favoring frustration
item.description: arXiv:2611.03837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the phase diagram and nature of the phase transitions of three-dimensional compact lattice Abelian Higgs models with negative gauge coupling. These models describe multicomponent complex scalar fields coupled to a compact U(1) gauge field. Negative gauge coupling favors frustrated plaquette configurations, competing with the tendency of the matter ferromagnetic-like interaction to suppress frustration. Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling analyses of models with one- and two-component scalar fields of unit charge reveal a substantially richer phase structure than at nonnegative gauge coupling. For two components, the O(3) transition line associated with gauge-invariant bilinear ordering extends into the negative-coupling region, and turns into a first-order transition line with decreasing $K$, toward the fully-frustrated $K\to -\infty$ limit. An analogous first-order transition line is also found for the one-component scalar matter with negative gauge coupling. Both one- and two-component models exhibit two additional continuous transition lines at sufficiently large matter coupling. Their energy-cumulant scaling is consistent with three-dimensional Ising and XY critical exponents, suggesting topological transitions in the $\mathbb Z_2$ and XY gauge universality classes, respectively. These results uncover additional phases generated by the competition between matter ordering and dynamical gauge frustration, whose physical characterization remains an open question.
item.dc:creator: Claudio Bonati, Ettore Vicari

item.title: Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz for the Toda chain from inverse scattering transform
item.description: arXiv:2611.03857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) procedure developed by Yang-Yang provides the free energy functional to be minimized via a variational problem. Their result not only gives the correct thermodynamics, but it also sets the framework for Generalized Hydrodynamics. Originally developed for quantum systems, this procedure has been recently successfully applied to (integrable) classical particle systems. However, this has never been done for classical field theories: no classical derivation has consistently accounted for solitons, breathers, radiation (dispersive modes), and their mutual interactions. We here derive the TBA equations for the Toda chain directly from its inverse scattering transform. This results in solitonic modes interacting with radiation, extending the soliton gas picture. We provide numerical verification of our equations against well established TBA equations in terms of particle modes. We expect the same procedure should apply to KdV, and pure radiative models as defocusing NLS and Sinh-Gordon, while we discuss current limitations in other models such as focusing NLS (and Ablowitz-Ladik) and Sine-Gordon.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Brollo

item.title: Maximum entropy explanation for the ubiquity of power-law mechanical responses
item.description: arXiv:2611.03999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ubiquitous power-law relaxation emerges from complex mechanical systems with a vast number of interacting exponential responses. Here we demonstrate that power-law responses satisfy a maximum entropy criterion, regulating the individual contributions under partial knowledge. This leads to a prediction that frequency range of validity decreases with power-law exponent, a property which is confirmed for some biological materials. The close relation with the fractional standard linear solid also leads to an incorporation of the equally ubiquitous stretched exponential behavior.
item.dc:creator: Sverre Holm

item.title: Capillary Coarsening Drives Re-entrant Statistical Transitions in Early Coffee-Ring Growth
item.description: arXiv:2611.04388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how nonequilibrium systems evolve between distinct statistical regimes remains a fundamental challenge in statistical physics. Here we show that particle deposition at an evaporating contact line provides an experimental realization of cooperative one-dimensional deposition, in which post-deposition capillary attraction drives particles to migrate, cluster, and coarsen. As deposition proceeds, the cluster-width distribution undergoes a striking re-entrant transition, evolving from an initial exponential form to a peaked Gamma distribution and subsequently returning to an exponential form. This dynamic transition is accompanied by a non-monotonic crossover in fluctuation scaling, $\sigma_w\sim\langle w\rangle^\kappa$, with $\kappa$ changing successively from $1$ to $1/2$ and back to $1$. Monte Carlo simulations reproduce these statistical transitions. Our results establish evaporative contact-line deposition as a simple model of correlated one-dimensional assembly and reveal how local interactions can produce re-entrant statistical behaviour in a nonequilibrium system.
item.dc:creator: Arundas Chandradasan, Dileep Mampallil

item.title: Critical amplitudes of the Baxter-Wu model from MCPA and Wolff simulations: free-exponent and fixed-exponent fits
item.description: arXiv:2611.04733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The two-dimensional Baxter-Wu model belongs to the universality class of the four-state Potts model. Exact expressions are available for its energy, specific heat, magnetization, and polarization amplitudes. We use these results as a benchmark for evaluating two simulation algorithms and two approaches to extracting critical amplitudes. Microcanonical population annealing (MCPA) and the sublattice-freezing Wolff algorithm yield highly consistent estimates for the energy and order parameters when applied to lattices of comparable size. According to the exact Joyce series, the local effective exponent does not stabilize at a constant value but instead undergoes a monotonic drift. This behaviour stems from corrections to scaling, which can be expressed as a series in the cube root of the reduced temperature. As a result, these corrections decay relatively slowly, with the leading term being of relative order $|t|^{2/3}$. When performing a fit with a free exponent on an automatically identified plateau, this drift gets incorporated into the estimated exponent, introducing a substantial bias in the derived amplitudes. In contrast, a fit that fixes the exponent to its exact value and explicitly accounts for the analytic correction series delivers a close match to the known exact amplitudes. Using this refined fitting approach, we obtain estimates for the susceptibility amplitudes and the universal amplitude ratios. These values are in good agreement with predictions from form-factor calculations. Additionally, we numerically determine the leading correction coefficient for the polarization.
item.dc:creator: Vyacheslav Mozolenko, Ian Pile, Lev Shchur

item.title: Stochastic synthesis and degradation of arbitrary diffusive processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.04843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Target search processes are often carried out by diffusive elements that are introduced and removed at random times, causing fluctuations in the number of searchers in the system over time. For instance, proteins are synthesized and degraded stochastically in the cell, and susceptible to react with specific binding sites during their lifetime. Here we derive the density profile generated by non-interacting particles subject to stochastic synthesis and degradation (SSD) at constant rates, given a source location and an arbitrary propagator for the single, non-degrading particle. We also study the first-passage properties of these many-searcher processes, which can be deduced from the knowledge of the first-passage time distribution of a single particle. We analyse the behaviours of the characteristic reaction time and of the mean first-passage time in the limits of small and large rates. Taking into account the costs associated with synthesis leads to the existence of an optimal synthesis rate. We further generalise these results to bursty synthesis, when production events involve more than one particle at a time, as often observed in cell biology. The mean first-passage time in these situations can be significantly reduced at low synthesis or large degradation rates, as it is divided by the mean burst size in these regimes. The results presented here are applied to one-dimensional Brownian searches. Some general connections between SSD and resetting processes are pointed out as well as important differences, since SSD is associated with a distinct queueing protocol.
item.dc:creator: Denis Boyer, Gabriel Mercado-V\'asquez

item.title: Real-Space renormalization for the drawups and drawdowns of stochastic trajectories: universality classes for diffusion processes and random walks via the scale function
item.description: arXiv:2611.04853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For one-dimensional diffusion processes with arbitrary diffusion coefficient $D(x)$ and Ito force $F_I(x)$, we analyze the statistical properties of the renormalized trajectories at scale $\Gamma$, where one keeps only the alternating sequence of local minima and local maxima that are separated by drawups and drawdowns of amplitude bigger than $\Gamma$. The elementary RG-step between $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma+d \Gamma$ thus amounts to eliminate the drawups and drawdowns of amplitude $\Gamma$, a real-space-RG-procedure that is well-known for Brownian trajectories in the context of the Strong-Disorder-RG approach applied to the disorder landscape of random models. The main result is that the universality classes are determined by the scale function $s(x)$ satisfying $D(x) s''(x)+F_I(x) s'(x)=0$ that governs the exit probabilities from an interval : all the diffusions sharing the same scale function $s(x)$ have the same statistics of renormalized trajectories, even if their initial microscopic trajectories are completely different. The simplest universality classes for diffusions on the whole line $x \in ]-\infty,+\infty[$ and on the half-line $x \in ]0,+\infty[$ are illustrated with several examples of processes, with or without steady states: Cauchy, Student, Bessel, Fisher-Snedecor, Geometric Brownian. This framework concerning diffusion processes is then adapted to discrete-time and to continuous-time random walks on the one-dimensional lattice with arbitrary nearest-neighbor jump probabilities or rates.
item.dc:creator: Cecile Monthus

item.title: Universality in Anomalous Diffusion: Power Laws and Faster-Decaying Tails
item.description: arXiv:2611.05258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong anomalous diffusion is often characterized by a piecewise-linear spectrum of the moments of displacement. The spectrum is characterized by the slopes $\theta$ and $\zeta$ for small and large moments, respectively, and by the crossover moment $q_c$ at which the slope changes. The exponents $\theta$ and $\zeta$ characterize the asymptotic scaling of the bulk and of the tails of the probability distribution function of displacements, respectively. Here, we adopt asymptotic theory to match the behaviors at intermediate scales. The resulting constraint explains how distributions with algebraic tails imply strong anomalous diffusion, and it relates $q_c$ to the corresponding power law. Our theory provides universal hyper-scaling relations between the exponents characterizing strong anomalous diffusion, and it yields explicit expressions for the leading-order corrections to the asymptotic power-law behavior of the moments of displacement. We also characterize finite-time corrections and propose a robust distribution-based method to estimate $\theta$, $\zeta$, and $q_c$. The findings are supported by numerical and analytical results for three paradigmatic models exhibiting strong anomalous diffusion. Finally, we show that power-law tails are not only sufficient but also necessary for this scenario: with a Gaussian, or generally fast-decaying, bulk and exponentially rare ballistic excursions, the spectrum of moments is single-linear, and the crossover to the apparent second branch drifts with the observation time. When the bulk is fast decaying and the tail is a power law, strong anomalous diffusion is still present, but the hyper-scaling relations among the exponents are violated.
item.dc:creator: Claudio Giberti, Alessandro Vezzani, Raffaella Burioni, Lamberto Rondoni

item.title: Crossover duality for the quantum long-range Ising chain: perturbation theory around the short-range endpoint and a DMRG test
item.description: arXiv:2611.05284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a weakly coupled description of the long-range transverse-field Ising chain near its short-range crossover at $s_*=7/4$, where the couplings decay as $r^{-1-s}$. The Ising conformal field theory is coupled to an instantaneous Gaussian field through $\sigma\chi$, extending the classical long-range Ising duality to quantum chains. The equal-time interaction generates a stress-tensor deformation that causes the velocity to run and renormalizes the dynamical critical exponent $z$. Conformal perturbation theory gives $z=1-0.720\,\delta+O(\delta^2)$, $1/\nu=(1+z)/2+O(\delta^2)$, and $\omega=\delta+O(\delta^2)$, with $\delta=s_*-s$. DMRG calculations on periodic chains of up to $128$ sites provide a consistency test using theoretical inputs for $1/\nu$ and $\omega$. After accounting for slow finite-size corrections, static and dynamical estimates of $z$ agree, supporting the crossover expansion at $s=1.5$ and a two-sided Pad\'e interpolation at $s=1$, $1.25$, and $1.5$.
item.dc:creator: Junchen Rong

item.title: Exact Rokhsar-Kivelson points hosting first-order phase transitions in $S=1$ compass models
item.description: arXiv:2611.05326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study $S=1$ compass models on the square and kagome lattices with bond-dependent bilinear and biquadratic interactions parametrized by an angle $\theta$. For compatible geometries, we determine the exact ground-state manifolds throughout the interval $\pi/4\leq\theta\leq3\pi/4$. At each endpoint, a product of on-site unitaries maps the Hamiltonian to the Laplacian of a configuration graph $\mathcal{G}$ in the $S=1$ Cartesian basis. These endpoints are exact Rokhsar-Kivelson (RK) points, with one ground state per dynamically connected component of $\mathcal{G}$. Each such state is an equal-amplitude superposition in the transformed basis and acquires configuration-dependent phases upon transforming back to the original basis. Both models possess $m=O(L)$ independent and mutually commuting conserved $\mathbb{Z}_2$ line charges, where $L$ is the linear system size, forcing a ground-state degeneracy of at least $2^m$ at the RK endpoints. Throughout the interior region, $\pi/4<\theta<3\pi/4$, the ground-state manifold on each lattice is instead spanned by two product states, both annihilated by the Hamiltonian. On both lattices, each RK endpoint also hosts a first-order transition into this intervening interior phase spanned by the two product states with long-range order.
item.dc:creator: Jay Pandey

item.title: Higher-order interactions renormalize the thermodynamic signature of neural population codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.05336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maximum-entropy models of neural recordings can be treated as Boltzmann distributions at a fictitious temperature $T$, with the fitted model at $T=1$. Their specific-heat peak grows with population size and approaches that temperature, which has been read as a sign of criticality. The case rests on pairwise models, yet retinal codes require higher-order interactions. The thermodynamics of a model with such interactions fitted cell by cell has not been computed. Here I compute it exactly for pairwise and third-order models of the same populations of up to $20$ retinal ganglion cells, in salamander and marmoset. The triplet terms, required by the held-out likelihood, shift the peak by more than the finite-sample bias, with opposite sign in the two retinas. The peak is lower and grows more slowly in salamander, higher and grows faster in marmoset, and lies closer to $T=1$ in both. An exact decomposition traces most of the shift to the energy variance across population spike counts. A constraint on the spike-count distribution alone reproduces all of it in salamander and over half in marmoset. A second recording of each species, re-binning, and a common-input surrogate show that the sign is set by the spike-count structure of a recording at its temporal resolution, not by species. The thermodynamic signature of a neural code is therefore set not by the data alone but by the interaction order of the model used to read it.
item.dc:creator: Narendra N. Hegade

item.title: Quantum Error Correction in Nearly Critical Toric Codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.05375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate quantum error correction protocols for topological codes deformed away from their stabilizer limits, particularly as they are pushed towards quantum phase transitions into trivial phases. Our focus is primarily on quantum information stored within the ground-state manifold of the transverse-field toric code (TFTC), subjected to independent bit-flip and phase-flip decoherence. Although the transverse field induces strong quantum fluctuations of $m$ anyons in the ground states, we show that projective measurements of the "bare" toric code stabilizers can nevertheless be used to construct an efficient decoding algorithm which exhibits a finite threshold to both types of decoherence, even when the transverse field is tuned infinitesimally close to the quantum critical point. Our construction of the optimal postmeasurement decoders---that is, the optimal decoders assuming that the stabilizers are first measured---crucially relies on the stoquastic nature of the TFTC Hamiltonian, which affords a description of its ground states in terms of a classical lattice gauge theory. Using stoquasticity, we first prove that stabilizer measurements act unitarily on the undecohered TFTC ground states to excellent approximation, and that the optimal postmeasurement decoder can be efficiently implemented via Monte Carlo simulation of a constrained lattice gauge theory. We then construct the optimal postmeasurement decoder for the TFTC states under bit-flip and phase-flip decoherence, where we numerically demonstrate a finite threshold close to the quantum critical point. We provide theoretical evidence (without a rigorous proof) that stabilizer measurements constitute an optimal decoding strategy in this setting. For phase-flip decoherence, we further prove that the optimal postmeasurement decoding threshold is independent of the transverse field strength throughout the topological phase.
item.dc:creator: Zack Weinstein, Samuel J. Garratt

item.title: Cooling more while dissipating less: anomalous tradeoffs from thermodynamic geometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.27948v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that, starting from the same state, optimal driving can sometimes reach a colder (or hotter) target in the same amount of time while dissipating less energy, or equivalently dissipate the same amount of energy in a shorter time. We study this counterintuitive phenomenon in the slow-driving regime of an open quantum system, where we name it Near-Equilibrium Anomalous Tradeoff (NEAT). We establish necessary conditions for its occurrence and show its underlying geometric origin. While NEAT is reminiscent of the well-known Mpemba effect, the two phenomena are distinct in general. We demonstrate NEAT in an exactly solvable qutrit model, as well as for d-dimensional birth-death dynamics with independently controlled energy levels. Finally, we show how NEAT can improve the performance of Carnot engines.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Canzio, Vasco Cavina, Salvatore Raia, Vito Vetrano, Matteo Scandi, Paolo Abiuso

item.title: Long-range entangled criticality from coherent errors
item.description: arXiv:2611.03811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We find that coherent error can induce a phase transition from the clean surface code phase into an extended long-range entangled critical regime with diverging Markov length. To demonstrate this, we establish two general results of independent interest. The first relates topology and quantum information to mixed-state entanglement: we show that when a noise channel acting on a topological code preserves a higher-form symmetry and nonzero coherent information, the noisy state for generic logical input is long-range entangled. The second generalizes the local recovery construction based on finite Markov length to any locally parameterized family, thus encompassing local Lindbladian evolution, coherent errors followed by syndrome dephasing, and thermal states. We apply these results to the honeycomb surface code, in which we find an extended long-range entangled critical regime that is a quasi-long-ranged counterpart of 1-form strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. As a byproduct of these studies, we relate the conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network model.
item.dc:creator: Amir-Reza Negari, Subhayan Sahu, Jan Behrends, Benjamin B\'eri, Timothy H. Hsieh

item.title: Non-Hermitian effective dynamics from post-selection protocols
item.description: arXiv:2611.03910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiple seemingly distinct frameworks are commonly proposed to explain the emergence of effective non-Hermitian dynamics in quantum systems coupled to an environment. Furthermore, it remains contested how to properly calculate expectation values or whether thermal equilibrium states exist in non-Hermitian systems. In this work, we show that Feshbach projection, the Lindblad master equation, and the ancilla approach can all be understood through the Kraus map formalism, leading to non-Hermitian time evolution if an appropriate post-selection procedure is enforced. After first deriving an exact expression for the conditional system dynamics, we discuss the approximations employed in each approach and the classes of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that can be obtained. Within this framework, we physically justify the consistency of the right-right formalism (as opposed to the biorthogonal one) for calculating expectation values. Finally, we demonstrate that the traditional notion of thermodynamic equilibrium is not applicable to general non-Hermitian systems. Consequently, stationary states are characterized as non-equilibrium steady states, which should not be conflated with system-projected thermal states of the system-environment composite.
item.dc:creator: Apostolos Siskou, Volker Meden

item.title: Negative Junction Logarithms in Scalar Multipartite Entanglement
item.description: arXiv:2611.04220v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A three-region junction in a free real relativistic scalar vacuum in $2+1$ dimensions yields a strictly negative logarithmic contribution to genuine tripartite R\'enyi multi-entropy for every integer $n\geq3$ and all nondegenerate sector angles. The replica subtraction exactly removes loop classes associated with a single interface. Surviving loops have positive, scale-independent weight, yielding a logarithm whose sign is fixed by the negative R\'enyi prefactor. The selector is empty at $n=2$. The flat-sheet Friedrichs prescription fixes the scalar operator at the nonmanifold replica apex. It yields a convergent angular spectral formula for the coefficient.
item.dc:creator: Chen-Te Ma

item.title: Topology Does Not Determine Defect Mobility in Active Polar Matter
item.description: arXiv:2611.04428v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Topological defects are commonly characterized by their charge, although defects with the same charge can have different internal morphologies. We study the annihilation of isolated $\pm1$ defect pairs in a two-dimensional compressible Toner--Tu model, varying the morphology of the $+1$ defect while keeping the initial charges and separation fixed. Activity produces a morphology-dependent mobility asymmetry: reversing the radial orientation of an aster reverses which defect travels farther, and asters show the strongest response. An early-time analysis reveals that the initial morphology selects distinct density modes whose gradients subsequently feed back on the polarization. Consistently, removing the density-gradient coupling strongly suppresses the asymmetry. These results establish defect morphology, in addition to topological charge, as a dynamical variable governing defect-pair motion in active polar matter.
item.dc:creator: Abhra Puitandy, Shradha Mishra

item.title: Amplified transport variability in granular slope flows near the critical angle
item.description: arXiv:2611.04440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mechanical disturbances such as seismic shaking can set a granular slope in motion. Understanding the resulting transport before arrest is important for predicting topographic change, assessing landslide hazards and controlling powder flows in industrial processes. Experiments show that smaller disturbances can trigger avalanches and larger areas are mobilized as slopes approach their stability limit. Yet how much transport varies between events under the same macroscopic conditions and forcing remains unclear. Here we use numerical simulations to show that transport variability is amplified near the critical angle. We apply identical basal pulses to static granular layers with the same macroscopic conditions but different initial particle configurations. Although the mean transport increases approximately in inverse proportion to the angular distance from the critical angle, the standard deviation increases even faster and can exceed the mean. Thus, identical forcing can produce widely different transport amounts. Deterministic constitutive laws that assign a unique response to given macroscopic conditions cannot capture this variability. We introduce fluctuations into the energy balance to develop a stochastic model that captures the main features of the broadening transport distribution. These results show that assessing transport near the critical angle requires considering its distribution, not just its mean, and motivate constitutive descriptions that incorporate fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: Fumiaki Nakai, Yuto Sasaki

item.title: Strain-Glass Dynamics in the Superionic Conductor Na$_3$PS$_4$
item.description: arXiv:2611.04547v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ionic conduction in solid-state electrolytes is conventionally described by mobile cations migrating through a static host lattice. Yet the fastest conductors are often the most disordered, and how disorder enhances transport remains unresolved at the mesoscale, inaccessible to ensemble-averaged probes. We use Bragg X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy to measure nanoscale structural dynamics of a single ball-milled Na$_3$PS$_4$ particle. We find that the cubic phase behaves as a strain glass: a frustrated configuration of three degenerate tetragonal variants with short-range order. Its domain-wall motion is stress-driven, crossing over irreversibly to thermally activated dynamics on annealing as residual milling stress is depleted. Rearrangements follow scale-free avalanche statistics, matching ferroelastic martensites but without external driving. The tetragonal polymorph shows none of these features and relaxes fifty times more slowly. These dynamics occur on timescales comparable to estimated ionic diffusion across the particle, indicating the host structure cannot be assumed static on transport-relevant timescales.
item.dc:creator: Erik S. Lamb, Nicol\`o D'Anna, Phillip Ridley, Nelson Hua, Ivan Zaluzhnyy, James Burrow, Emilio Escauriza, Robin Glefke, Boyan K. Stoychev, Mingze Wan, Zhe Ren, Fabian Westermeier, Michael Sprung, Alex Fra\~n\'o, Ying Shirley Meng, Oleg G. Shpyrko

item.title: Designing turbulence through hierarchies
item.description: arXiv:2611.04706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Turbulence is defined by a set of emergent and singular phenomena: a constant-flux energy cascade, intermittency, a dissipation rate that survives the vanishing of viscosity, and the spontaneous loss of determinism of the inviscid limit. Which physical ingredients produce them remains unclear, because in fluids they always come together with incompressibility, spatial structure and vortex dynamics. Here we show that a hierarchy of inertia, coupled by the purely geometric nonlinearity of rigid constraints, is enough. A planar chain of rigid pendula whose lengths and masses decrease geometrically, coupled only through nearest-neighbor constraints, develops a far-from-equilibrium cascade that replaces thermal equipartition, with statistically local and time-irreversible energy transfer despite intrinsically nonlocal coupling. Its fluctuations are intermittent, yet self-similarity is restored by a hidden scale symmetry. As the viscosity vanishes, the dissipation rate saturates at a finite value, and thermal noise consistent with fluctuation-dissipation balance is amplified from the smallest to the largest scales within a fraction of a large-scale period. Because the hierarchy can be tuned and the same dynamics can be realized mechanically or electrically, turbulence becomes a property that can be designed and measured in the laboratory.
item.dc:creator: Flavio Tuteri, Andr\'e Freitas

item.title: Operational Thresholds for Long-Range Entanglement in Quantum Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.05069v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum networks distribute entanglement between distant nodes by combining many short entangled links using local quantum operations. These operations only succeed probabilistically, yet existing percolation-based theories of entanglement transmission treat them as perfect. We approach the problem through statistical physics, using a stochastic generalization of concurrence percolation to determine how reliable local operations must be for long-range entanglement to remain possible. On hierarchical $(U,V)$-flower networks, which permit full analytical control across network scales, we derive an exact renormalization recursion for the probability that an end-to-end entangled connection survives. For the $(2,2)$-flower this yields a closed-form operational phase boundary, $\eta_p = 2 - \frac{32}{27}\eta_s$, where $\eta_s$ and $\eta_p$ are the success probabilities of the series (entanglement swapping) and parallel (purification) operations, respectively. At this boundary the survival probability jumps discontinuously from $0$ to $S_\infty = 3/(4\eta_s)$. Numerically propagating the full distribution of end-to-end concurrence yields a second threshold in the initial link quality, which varies continuously with operational reliability. Above both thresholds the large-network state is binary: the connection either fails outright or approaches a perfect Bell pair. Our results thus reveal a two-threshold structure for long-range entanglement, in which operational reliability and initial link quality can compensate one another. Operational success rates therefore emerge alongside initial link quality as a primary design constraint for scalable quantum networks.
item.dc:creator: Arn Caesar, Xinqi Hu, Kim Christensen

item.title: How symmetry and complexity shape three-dimensional programmable self-assembly
item.description: arXiv:2611.05301v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-assembly enables complex structures to emerge from simple building blocks through local interaction rules. Are some structures intrinsically easier to design, that is, do they admit more sets of assembly rules than others? And, can this be predicted from their geometry? We address these questions using a three-dimensional polycube model with programmable face-to-face binding, defining a structure's assembly rule probability as the chance that a randomly chosen rule set produces it. For polycubes, this probability decreases exponentially with assembly complexity, the minimum information required to specify a structure's assembly rules. Intuitively, this follows because structures with low assembly complexity are generated not only by minimal rule sets but also by numerous more elaborate ones, and so arise disproportionately often. Symmetry can reduce assembly complexity by allowing the same building blocks and local interactions to be reused across different parts of a structure. Indeed, we find that the highest probability structures come from a tiny subset of highly symmetric structures. However, symmetry alone does not determine assembly complexity. Structures with the same symmetry can differ substantially in the amount of assembly information they require, depending on how effectively their global symmetry can be exploited by local growth rules. Overall, our results link information, symmetry, and assembly rule probability and suggest that identifying which geometric features permit rule reuse is central to designing minimal programmable self-assembling systems.
item.dc:creator: Prarthana Agrawal, Joakim Bohlin, Ard A. Louis

item.title: Percolation transition of strongly connected clusters in finite dimensions and on complete graphs
item.description: arXiv:2605.16987v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the percolation of strongly connected clusters (SCCs), in which sites are mutually reachable through directed paths, in systems with randomly oriented bonds by extensive simulations on hypercubic lattices from dimensions $d=2$ to $7$ and on complete graphs. Below the upper critical dimension $d_u=6$, critical SCCs exhibit a nontrivial fractal dimension $d_{\rm SCC}$ with a nonmonotonic dependence on dimension: $d_{\rm SCC}$ reaches a maximum at $d=4$, in contrast to the fractal dimension of ordinary percolation clusters, which increases monotonically with $d$. The SCC size distribution follows $\sim s^{-\tau_{\rm SCC}}$, where the Fisher exponent is consistent with the hyperscaling relation $\tau_{\rm SCC}=1+d/d_{\rm SCC}$ and, unlike $d_{\rm SCC}$ itself, increases monotonically with $d$. For $d\geq d_u$, mean-field behavior is recovered with $d_{\rm SCC}/d=1/3$, consistent with complete-graph results. However, unlike finite-dimensional lattices, complete graphs exhibit a double-scaling structure in the SCC size distribution: large SCCs are governed by the mean-field exponent $\tau_{\rm SCC}=4$, while small SCCs follow a distinct power law with exponent $\tau'=1$. At $d_u=6$, logarithmic corrections are also observed. These results show that SCCs remain well-defined fractal objects across dimensions, exhibiting both a nontrivial dimensional dependence and a nontrivial crossover from finite-dimensional to mean-field behavior.
item.dc:creator: Qi Wang, Ming Li

item.title: Competition for Survival and the Law of Maximum Entropy Production
item.description: arXiv:2605.27457v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The law of maximum entropy production (LMEP) is a selection principle stating that a non-equilibrium system will select the path or assembly of paths out of available paths that minimizes the potential or maximizes the entropy at the fastest rate given the constraints. Precise quantitative experimental tests are desirable for LMEP verification. Here we report electrical-circuit experiments on suspensions of silver particles which self-organize under electric field, form conducting paths and thus generate entropy by Joule heating. Our experiments on parallel-connected pairs of samples demonstrate a competitive relationship, thereby supporting the selection of the most efficient path. We find: (1) With sufficient voltage, a conducting bundle of silver particles forms, which acts as a self-organized dissipative structure (SODS). (2) With two samples in parallel, usually only one can develop SODS, due to the competition effect. As one sample approaches the maximum EPR, the others EPR is near zero. This confirms the path selection principle: only the highest EPR path survives. (3) At the end of the evolution, the sum of the sample EPR and the power supply circuit EPR approaches the calculated maximum. The deviation from the maximum is slightly lower when there are two competing samples. We identify the selection mechanism enabling natural selection and LMEP: A SODS gains a form of physical "fitness" when it establishes a pathway that efficiently suppresses the driving thermodynamic potential. As it develops and approaches the maximum EPR, the SODS modifies its nonequilibrium environment by consuming available free energy and eliminating the gradients that could support alternative pathways. We also examine the global implications of LMEP and propose that it serves as a driving mechanism propelling the hypothetical ascent of civilizations along the Kardashev scale.
item.dc:creator: Albert Han, Jiri Kataman-Kustwan, Alexey Bezryadin

item.title: Measurement-induced spatially nonuniform fluctuations of the local particle number and their crossover in a quasiperiodic free-fermion chain
item.description: arXiv:2607.03799v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study continuously monitored dynamics of a quasiperiodic free-fermion chain defined on a Fibonacci lattice. We focus on fluctuations of the local particle number, which do not exhibit quasiperiodic spatial modulation in the unitary limit. Remarkably, we demonstrate that they exhibit a nonuniform spatial pattern originating from the quasiperiodic long-range order under continuous measurement. Furthermore, employing both physicaland perpendicular-space analyses, we elucidate that a measurement-induced crossover emerges in fluctuations due to the interplay between the incommensurate modulation and the continuous measurement. While weak measurement yields a distribution reflecting the long-range spatial structure of the quasiperiodic system, an increase in measurement strength alters the distribution into one dominated by the local environment of each site. A structure-factor analysis further reveals that the weak-measurement regime is characterized by two dominant Bragg peaks corresponding to the golden-mean modulation, whereas the strong-measurement regime exhibits the characteristic Bragg-peak hierarchy of the Fibonacci pattern. We also elucidate that the measurement-induced crossover emerges in other physical quantities such as connected correlation functions. These findings offer insights into nonequilibrium quasiperiodic phenomena emerging in continuously monitored dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Toranosuke Matsubara, Kazuki Yamamoto

item.title: Entanglement Asymmetry in Random Quantum Automata
item.description: arXiv:2607.07556v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the subsystem entanglement asymmetry in random quantum automaton ensembles, which are generated by permuting the basis states in the Hilbert space and applying global phase shifts. We compute the ensemble average of the $U(1)$ subsystem asymmetry in different connectivity geometries, showing that the late-time limit of the ensemble associated to a 2-local circuit geometry coincides with the all-to-all ensemble average. By focusing on different subsystem sizes, we demonstrate that, similarly to Haar-random circuits, the system locally symmetrizes. However, in sharp contrast to the Haar-random setting, the scale at which symmetrization happens depends on the initial state, a phenomenon we associate with the interplay of conservation of the participation entropy and the uniform exploration of charge sectors. Additionally, we connect the growth of the subsystem asymmetry to the subsystem coherence and show that their growth is characterized by the same symmetrization scale.
item.dc:creator: Olalla A. Castro-Alvaredo, D\'avid Sz\'asz-Schagrin, Michele Mazzoni

item.title: Strongly-connected percolation on directed lattices
item.description: arXiv:2607.24975v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study percolation on lattices with directed bonds, focusing on the behavior of strongly-connected percolation clusters -- clusters in which every site is reachable from every other along a directed path. We consider the two-dimensional square lattice and various globally isotropic arrangements of the directions of the bonds. Performing simulations using a range of algorithmic approaches, we calculate high-precision values for critical exponents, fractal dimensions, crossing probabilities, and percolation thresholds for bond percolation with each bond arrangement. We find that the critical behavior is in a distinctly different universality class from that of traditional undirected percolation, but that all bond arrangements appear to fall in the same universality class.
item.dc:creator: M. E. J. Newman, P. Grassberger, R. M. Ziff

item.title: Chemical potentials from structure factors: II. Charged multi-component mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2608.30060v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The chemical potentials of charged multi-component mixtures are central to electrolyte thermodynamics, but remain difficult to compute from atomistic simulations. The S0 method enables computing chemical potentials of mixtures from equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations. Here we extend the S0 method to charged mixtures by combining the composition-space framework developed in Part I: Neutral Multi-component Mixtures with a Coulombic treatment of the small-wavenumber limits of static structure factors. This approach separates thermodynamically relevant neutral composition fluctuations from forbidden macroscopic charge fluctuations, and further accounts for charge-neutrality constraints. We use the method to compute the chemical potentials of multiple-halide aqueous salt solutions, elucidating the ion-specific thermodynamic effects. We also calculate the mixing free energies of molten salt mixtures, demonstrating the importance of correctly describing long-wavelength electrostatic correlations.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Wang, Roya Savoj, Musahid Ahmed, Bingqing Cheng

item.title: Distinguishability Transitions from Global Quantum Snapshots
item.description: arXiv:2609.09296v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum states generated by generic time evolution are locally featureless: local measurements return random outcomes that are identical for all states. However, global snapshots in the computational basis are surprisingly effective at distinguishing between quantum states. We explore the ability of Bayesian classifiers to discriminate between many random quantum states using a small number of measurement outcomes. We identify a phase transition in the ability of the classifier to distinguish between $k$ candidate states with $m$ shots controlled by the variable $x = m / \ln k$, and derive the threshold value $x_c$. We extend our results to low-depth circuits near the onset of anti-concentration, as well as to noisy circuits and phase-random states.
item.dc:creator: Catherine McCarthy, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, Romain Vasseur

item.title: Intrinsic non-Markovian magnetisation dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2512.07378v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Memory effects are widespread in complex systems while evidence of non-Markovian dynamics in fundamental physical systems has been limited to specifically engineered cases. Here we report on the experimental observation of non-Markovian magnetisation dynamics in crystalline cobalt. Intense terahertz electromagnetic driving brings the system into a non-equilibrium state, and allows us to follow its magnetisation dynamics in real time at low temperatures. The response reveals a striking multi-peaked frequency spectrum that defies conventional descriptions. Using open quantum system theory we evidence that a non-Markovian memory kernel, arising from spin-phonon bath coupling, naturally explains both the spectral structure and its temperature dependence. Theoretical prediction of the spectrum is accomplished by simulating the non-Markovian Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, while analytics quantitatively determines the frequencies of three spectral peaks. The results demonstrate that intrinsic memory effects can emerge in a simple ferromagnet, opening new opportunities to explore and control non-Markovian dynamics in condensed-matter systems.
item.dc:creator: Felix Hartmann, Vivek Unikandanunni, Matias Bargheer, Eric E. Fullerton, Stefano Bonetti, Janet Anders

item.title: Topological phase transition of deformed ${\mathbb Z}_3$ toric code
item.description: arXiv:2603.09107v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate topological phase transitions in a family of deformed $\mathbb Z_3$ toric-code wavefunctions prepared from a cluster state by local deformations and projective measurements. Their norms map to the $Q=3$ Potts model for single-parameter deformations and to a three-state Ashkin--Teller-like (AT$_3$) construction with two independent four-spin couplings in the general case. Projected entangled-pair-state (PEPS) and variational uniform matrix-product-state (VUMPS) calculations identify the toric-code (TC) phase and phases in which electric ($e$) anyons are confined or condensed. These phases are separated by critical structures with central charges $c=4/5$, $8/5$, and isolated $c=1$ antiferromagnetic (AFM) endpoints. A normalized finite-distance $e$-anyon pair-state norm provides a Fredenhagen--Marcu-type check of the confinement boundary, while the topological data of the quantum double $D(\mathbb Z_3)$ imply a topological entanglement entropy $\gamma=\log3$ throughout the gapped toric-code phase. Relative to the $\mathbb Z_2$ case, the absence of sign-change folding leaves the AFM endpoints unfolded, and the extreme deformation reaches square ice with an emergent $U(1)$ one-form symmetry, Hilbert-space fragmentation, and exact scar configurations.
item.dc:creator: Yun-Tak Oh, Hyun-Yong Lee

item.title: Measurement and feedback-driven adaptive dynamics in the classical and quantum kicked top
item.description: arXiv:2604.19874v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In classical dynamical systems, stochastic feedback can stabilize otherwise unstable periodic orbits, giving rise to distinct controlled and uncontrolled phases as the rate of control application is varied. In this work, we apply these control protocols in classical, semiclassical, and quantum regimes to the kicked top, a paradigmatic model of quantum chaos. The quantum kicked top, modeled as the dynamics of a spin-S object, naturally interpolates between these regimes with the spin size S acting as an effective Planck constant. We show that the dynamics of the kicked top in classical, semiclassical, and fully quantum limits can all be controlled using stochastic feedback protocols. Comparing the full quantum dynamics to a truncated Wigner approximation that captures quantum noise but neglects interference beyond the Ehrenfest time, we find that low-moment observables are largely accounted for semiclassically, while higher moments retain a discrepancy that peaks at the control transition, consistent with contributions from interference and possibly nonlinearities in rare trajectories that explore the compact phase space. We also find rapid purification in the numerics studied for all rates of control considered, suggesting that control quenches the top's ability to encode a qubit of quantum information even in the uncontrolled phase.
item.dc:creator: Mahaveer Prasad, Ahana Chakraborty, Thomas Iadecola, Manas Kulkarni, J. H. Pixley, Sriram Ganeshan, Justin H. Wilson

item.title: Thermalization with Gaussian Quantum Cellular Automata
item.description: arXiv:2606.05542v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the long-time dynamics of many-body bosonic lattice systems under translation-invariant Gaussian quantum cellular automata. We formulate two sets of conditions on GQCAs which separately guarantee thermalization of any state on the local Weyl algebra to the infinite temperature state, whenever the state is locally normal and has uniformly bounded particle density. Our main intermediate result is a quantum many-body generalization of the classic Riemann-Lebesgue lemma which is a bound on expectation values of local Weyl operators involving their support and the state's particle density.
item.dc:creator: Roman Geiko, Jake Gerenraich

item.title: Generating functions and efficient numerical simulation of aggregation-fragmentation kinetics
item.description: arXiv:2606.10785v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we review and revisit the generating function techniques that provide exact analytical solutions for aggregation and fragmentation equations across several physical regimes including spontaneous and collisional shattering. For discrete coagulation-fragmentation equations with size-independent rates under monodisperse initial conditions, we show the derivation of several explicit closed-form solutions. We also briefly report the exact solutions for continuous, three-particle, $D$-particle collisions and two-component generalizations. Source-driven aggregation yields steady distributions featuring a universal $s^{-3/2}$ power-law decay and a cutoff mass scaling $s_{*} \sim t^{2}$. We also remind that exploitation of the low-rank representations of the aggregation kernel allows to organize efficient modelling the aggregation kinetics and extend this idea showing a simple way for the fast accounting of the spontaneous framentation terms. We exploit our numerical algorithm and study the numerical solutions for multiple models of spontaneous fragmentation and find a new example of temporal oscillations for the closed aggregation-fragmentation process.
item.dc:creator: S. A. Matveev

item.title: Equilibration of generalized subsystems: a quantum-channel approach
item.description: arXiv:2606.18360v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum systems governed by unitary and reversible microscopic dynamics may nevertheless exhibit equilibration, in the sense that some effective description becomes time-independent. Standard equilibration results usually consider two separate situations: system-environment structures, in which the composite system evolves unitarily while the system of interest equilibrates, and restricted measurements, such as coarse-grained POVMs and observables, in which the measurement statistics equilibrate. Here, we bring these descriptions into a common state-level framework using the concept of generalized subsystems, where the accessible effective state appears as the output of a quantum channel acting on the microscopic state. We derive bounds showing that generalized subsystems equilibrate when their dimension is small compared with the effective dimension of the discarded microscopic information. We further show that this condition is met for typical initial states in large subspaces and that the resulting equilibrium description is largely insensitive to microscopic initial details. The framework recovers the usual equilibration bounds for ordinary subsystems and finite families of POVMs. As an example, we also introduce a finite-resolution energy channel that maps unresolved microscopic energy levels into effective energy levels, thereby making residual effective coherences explicit and showing how spectral multiplicities constrain those coherences while strengthening equilibration. Our results provide a unified state-level formulation of quantum equilibration under general forms of limited accessible information.
item.dc:creator: Pedro S. Correia, Adalberto D. Varizi, Gabriel Dias Carvalho

item.title: Open-ended innovation arm-race in zero-sum games
item.description: arXiv:2607.25677v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We discuss zero-sum games with open-ended innovation, whereby each player may introduce new strategies. The innovation process is modeled as a draw of new strategies form a distribution. It is argued that, when the cost of innovation is vanishingly small, this setting can lead to an everlasting innovation arm-race. In particular, the introduction of new technologies of the advanced player increases the marginal utility for technological innovation of the backward one, whereas innovation of the backward player discourages the more advanced one to innovate.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Marsili, Leandro Chaves Rego

item.title: State preparation and detection for quantum simulation of particle collisions
item.description: arXiv:2607.26142v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simulating the real-time dynamics of particle collisions is a promising application of quantum simulators, because classical methods such as tensor networks struggle to capture the highly entangled states generated in high-energy scattering. Realizing such simulations requires both the preparation of incoming wave packets and the detection of the outgoing scattering products. In this work, we propose protocols that address both challenges on programmable analog and digital quantum simulation platforms. Our state-preparation scheme uses a weakly coupled auxiliary qubit - or, more generally, a customized local quench - to inject a single quasiparticle with well-defined momentum. Because it relies only on conservation of energy, this scheme requires no fine-tuning or prior knowledge about particle eigenstates, making it robust against errors in calibration and implementation. The momenta of scattering products are then extracted, using only local measurements, from the interference pattern that arises when particles are reflected at the system's boundary. We validate our protocols through numerical simulations, first in a simple single-particle model and subsequently in two interacting many-body systems: a Rydberg atom chain and an Ising chain in a mixed field. We demonstrate how high-energy regimes, necessary to access inelastic scattering processes, can be reached through an adiabatic ramp, and how the wave packet shape can be optimized by spatially modulating the Hamiltonian. Finally, we show how the protocol can be generalized to systems with more than one spatial dimension. Our proposal provides a versatile approach to the quantum simulation of scattering phenomena, and is compatible with several quantum simulation platforms that are already experimentally available.
item.dc:creator: Federica Maria Surace, Sary Bseiso, John Preskill

item.title: Chemical potentials from structure factors: I. Neutral multi-component mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2608.08357v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The chemical potentials of multi-component mixtures underlie many physical and chemical phenomena, but remain challenging to compute. The S0 method enables the computation of chemical potentials from equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, by leveraging the thermodynamic relationship between particle number fluctuations and derivatives of chemical potentials, followed by numerical integration along different compositions. Here we generalize the S0 method from two-component mixtures to neutral multi-component mixtures. We first extend the statistical mechanical formalism to high-dimensional compositional space, and then introduce a Gaussian process integration scheme combined with active learning to efficiently integrate chemical potentials and sample diverse compositions. We use this method to compute the mixing free energies of a molten metal alloy, and the solubilities of two paracetamol polymorphs in water-ethanol solvents. The extended S0 method provides a practical and scalable route for computing chemical potentials in neutral bulk multi-component mixtures from atomistic simulations.
item.dc:creator: Roya Savoj, Xiaoyu Wang, Musahid Ahmed, Bingqing Cheng

item.title: Statistical levels and spatial modes of Fock-space heterogeneity in many-body localization crossovers
item.description: arXiv:2609.15323v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Near many-body localization crossovers, local memory fluctuates strongly among eigenstates and ensemble realizations, but the observed heterogeneity combines contributions from different statistical levels. We develop a statistical framework based on configuration-space distance distributions that uses a variance decomposition to separate fluctuations within eigenstates, between eigenstates of one sample, and between samples. Applying this framework to random-cosine and quasiperiodic-cosine Ising ensembles with the same one-site field marginal, we find that, at the exact-diagonalization sizes studied, the clearest difference occurs among disorder realizations or quasiperiodic phase samples, whereas within-eigenstate and within-sample eigenstate-to- eigenstate contributions remain broadly comparable. Spatial covariances show that random outer fluctuations have a much stronger uniform component, whereas quasiperiodic phase fluctuations are organized more strongly at finite wave number and partly cancel in the spatial average controlling the distance center. We find that, near the crossover in the random ensemble, the ensemble-averaged distance center is particularly sensitive to changes in the nominal field strength. Combined with sample-to-sample differences in the realized field amplitude, this mean response accounts for much of the sample-to-sample variation in the distance center. Analysis of half-chain entanglement further shows that its sample-to-sample fluctuations likewise reflect the combined effects of amplitude variations and its own mean response. An application to a fixed-magnetization spin chain demonstrates the framework in a constrained configuration space. Resolving both statistical level and spatial mode therefore provides a more complete picture of sample- dependent many-body memory and its configuration-space probability geometry.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Jing Liu, Chen Cheng

item.title: Dynamic clustering of active chemotactic Janus particles
item.description: arXiv:2610.26657v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modeling self-propulsion as an emergent diffusiophoretic effect, we come back to the dynamic clustering experiment of active Janus colloids. Working in the original three-dimensional geometry, and using the chemical solute concentration as a control parameter, we find that the dynamic clustering region occupies a robust fraction of the phase diagram. This behavior is rationalized using a linear stability analysis that efficiently captures the instability of the gas phase to dynamic clusters. We also find that dynamic clustering results from the combined effects of a Keller-Segel collapse and of a motility-induced phase separation, either being arrested by the orientational coupling to the chemical field in agreement with previous work.
item.dc:creator: Jo\"el Mabillard, Fr\'ed\'eric van Wijland, Jean-Baptiste Fournier
